Chapter 3: The Hidden Costs of Obedience and Submission
You know, obedience is something we’re taught to admire. From the time we’re kids, most of us are told to listen to authority, follow the rules, and show respect to the people in charge. It sounds like a recipe for harmony and order, right? But there’s another side to this story—one that doesn’t get talked about nearly enough.
Picture a family at the dinner table. On the surface, everything looks warm and happy—polite conversation, laughter floating around. But underneath, there’s an undercurrent of tension. The father, respected and stern, sets the tone for the whole house. His opinions are rarely, if ever, questioned. His decisions? They’re accepted without a word. The kids quickly figure out it’s safer to nod along than to rock the boat, so their real feelings stay hidden.
And it’s not just families where this happens. You’ll see it in offices, schools, even whole communities. The person with the most power makes the rules, and everyone else follows. If someone does speak out or push back, they’re seen as a problem—or worse, they’re pushed to the fringes. So, most folks keep quiet, do what’s expected, and avoid standing out.
Here’s the thing—this kind of obedience comes at a cost. When people are too scared to speak up, individuality and creativity get smothered. Think about it: How many great ideas have never seen the light of day because someone was afraid to share them? When disagreement is punished, progress just… stalls. The world ends up being a place where only those with the loudest voices are heard, and everyone else fades quietly into the background.
Let me share a real example. Imagine a nurse working in a busy hospital. She spots a mistake in a patient’s chart—something that could have serious consequences. But the doctor in charge? He’s got a reputation for losing his temper when questioned. The nurse has seen what happens to people who challenge him. So, she hesitates. Should she speak up or stay silent? In the end, her fear wins out, and she hopes someone else will catch the error.
This kind of submission isn’t just about being afraid of getting in trouble. Sometimes, it’s just habit. We’re taught to trust authority, to believe that the people in charge know best. And most of the time, we don’t even stop to question it—even when the facts tell a different story.
But the price we pay for this obedience is steep. Mistakes happen. Opportunities are missed. People start to feel powerless, just waiting for someone else to take the lead. Over time, you might even lose confidence in your own judgment. It becomes easier to let others make decisions for you.
But what really hurts is what happens inside. When you keep giving in, over and over, you start to lose respect for yourself. You begin to doubt your own worth, thinking you’re just not as capable or important as those calling the shots. And before you know it, those doubts shape your choices, and limit what you believe you can do.
So, how do you break out of this pattern? It takes more than just courage. You’ve got to be willing to question authority, to trust your own instincts, and to take responsibility for your actions. You have to remember that leaders are just people—they make mistakes, they have blind spots. And your voice matters, even if it goes against the grain.
Not everyone is ready to take that leap. It’s easier to just follow the path that’s been set out for you. But for those who do—who choose to step up and speak out—the rewards are incredible. You find a sense of agency and purpose that can’t come from simply obeying. And you realize that real respect isn’t about submission—it’s about understanding each other and sharing responsibility.
